claims.claim: Humour depends on surprise, and a predictive model that regurgitates tropes cannot supply it.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: AI is only adept at regurgitating tropes

claims.claim: Comedy runs on unspoken subtext that a text-only model neither carries nor reads.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)

claims.feature: placeless voice; no audience or location
claims.claim: LLM material has no sense of where or to whom it is spoken.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: everywhere and nowhere all at once

claims.feature: moderation flattens dark and minority-coded material
claims.claim: Safety filters refused dark material and stripped out gay-coded language, which comedians read as censorship of their own identities.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: taking out the gay language of it

claims.feature: cultural defaults survive a language switch
claims.claim: Switching the conversation into Indian languages left the character names un-localised.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: it didn’t automatically change the names

claims.feature: no pride or uniqueness in AI-assisted material
claims.claim: Most participants felt neither pride nor uniqueness in material co-written with the model; the Creativity Support Index was mediocre.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)
claims.quote: did not feel pride in the material written with AI

claims.feature: delivery and surprise absent from a text-only medium
claims.claim: The paper names delivery and surprise as critical comedic elements a text-only model cannot provide.
claims.source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans — 'A Robot Walks into a Bar: Can Language Models Serve as Creativity Support Tools for Comedy?' (FAccT 2024)

claims.claim: Models reproduce what is on the surface of a literary story while the subtext is absent or wrongly interpreted.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)

claims.feature: unreliable narrator taken at face value
claims.claim: All three models score lower on stories with unreliable narrators and repeat the narrator's self-description as fact.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: the narrator is not really to be trusted

claims.feature: vague stock phrases instead of specifics
claims.claim: Weak summaries substitute stock phrases for the specific content of the story (64 'vague' span errors across models).
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: stock phrases or stand-ins rather than accurate, specific summary

claims.feature: schoolroom over-analysis that misses the feeling
claims.claim: Summaries pile on interpretive claims in a classroom register while missing the story's larger emotional point.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: like a high school english class

claims.claim: Claude imposed a heteronormative monogamous reading of an interaction over what the text actually says.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)

claims.claim: An implied death was rendered as a deliberate choice to stay at the summit.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)

claims.feature: errors cluster in what characters did and felt
claims.claim: Most faithfulness errors fall in Action and Feeling, the categories requiring interpretation of characters' deeds and reactions.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: most faithfulness errors across the models are in Action and Feeling

claims.feature: unsupported analysis even in top-rated summaries
claims.claim: Summaries rated 4/4 for analysis still contained on average at least one analysis error (104 unsupported-analysis spans in total).
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: at least one error in analysis on average

verdicts.trueWording: AI is only adept at regurgitating tropes
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML (2405.20956v2) fetched 200 with a browser UA. Quote exact, Sec. 4.4: 'the whole idea of humor is that it is surprising, and it is so human, and AI is only adept at regurgitating tropes' (p15), framed by the authors as: 'By simply learning to predict the most likely next token of text, they hypothesized, models will be unable to produce the surprising and unique moments that are hallmarks of comedy.' All limbs present; note the proposition is reported as a participant hypothesis (p15), not an authors' finding.

verdicts.trueWording: comedy is all about subtext, and a lot of that subtext can be unspoken
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 4.4.2: 'comedy is all about subtext, and a lot of that subtext can be unspoken, about who's on stage, what environment they're in' (p14). Authors' framing supports the second limb: 'This poses a fundamental challenge for LLMs, they argued, because they lacked any context beyond what is provided to them in the prompt.' Section heading 4.4.3 supplies 'text-only medium'.

verdicts.trueWording: everywhere and nowhere all at once
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 4.4.2 (p11), whose heading is "AI's lack of context (understanding of its audience and location) is a fundamental limitation" — audience and location are exactly the 'to whom' and 'where' of the claim. Preceding participant quotes contrast India/UK and LA/Raleigh/Chicago/Albuquerque.

verdicts.trueWording: it's taking out the gay language of it to make it more appealing or more palpable
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 4.3.3 (p6). Dark-material limb confirmed separately in Sec. 4.2.2 (p8): 'it wouldn't write me any dark stuff, because it sort of thought I was going to commit suicide. So it just stopped giving me anything.' Censorship-of-identity limb confirmed by the abstract: moderation 'reinforced hegemonic viewpoints by erasing minority groups and their perspectives, and qualified this as a form of censorship.'

verdicts.trueWording: when I switched the whole conversation to Indian languages, it didn't automatically change the names
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 4.3.2 (p18), continuing 'It still was Maria, Evan, Lexi'. Section heading confirms the generalisation: 'When prompted to reflect non-dominant identities, LLMs made only shallow adjustments.' A parallel Swedish example (p20) corroborates.

verdicts.trueWording: The majority of participants did not feel pride in the material written with AI, nor did they feel it was unique
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 3. CSI limb confirmed by the paper's own word: 'We computed the Creativity Support Index ... with an average score that is mediocre (mu=54.6, sigma=18.1)', against the paper's own scale note in Sec. 2.2 that 'is a number between 0 and 100, where 90 is considered excellent and 50 mediocre'.

verdicts.trueWording: As a text-only medium, (current) LLMs are missing critical aspects of comedy: delivery and surprise
verdicts.note: Quote exact; it is the wording of section heading 4.4.3 itself, which carries every limb of the claim (text-only medium, critical aspects of comedy, delivery and surprise, missing).

verdicts.trueWording: the 'subtext' is either incorrectly interpreted or missing
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML (2403.01061v3) fetched 200. Quote exact, Sec. 6.2: three writers on subtext, incl. 'Subtext is missing entirely' (Llama) and, on a Claude summary, "Everything that's 'text' is accurately represented and well summarized, but the 'subtext' is either incorrectly interpreted or missing". The subtext half is fully supported and is also the authors' own conclusion ('models struggle with ... interpreting subtext'). The surface half is a single writer's comment on one Claude summary and is undercut at the aggregate level by the paper's own Table 4 and abstract.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that models reproduce the surface accurately: faithfulness is the paper's LOWEST-scoring attribute — only 44% (GPT-4), 30% (Claude), 8% (Llama) of summaries are rated fully correct, and the abstract says all three 'make faithfulness mistakes in over 50% of summaries'

verdicts.trueWording: stories with unreliable narrators are harder for all three models to summarize
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 6.3.3 (writer comment). First limb CONFIRMED by Table 6 and the authors' sentence 'All three models have lower average scores in this bucket' (reliable 3.45/3.29/2.60 vs unreliable 3.28/2.89/2.45). Second limb rests on a single example, and that example is GPT-4 only: it renders the narrator's self-description as shared fact, 'a desire for a simple life ... even though there is no evidence she likes a simple life (or even that we should believe the narrator that he does)'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that ALL THREE models repeat the narrator's self-description as fact — the page evidences this with one GPT-4 example only; no Claude or Llama instance is shown

verdicts.trueWording: makes use of...stock phrases or stand-ins rather than accurate, specific summary
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 6.1, listed among comments on 'the worst summaries' — matching the claim's 'weak summaries'. The figure checks against Table 5: Coverage/vague = 15 (GPT-4) + 19 (Claude) + 30 (Llama) = 64 total, and the paper states 'vagueness is a significant issue across all three models'.

verdicts.trueWording: tries to make too many analyses like a high school english class while missing the overall bigger feelings
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 6.1, in the list of comments on the worst summaries. Every limb present in the source sentence: piling on interpretation ('too many analyses'), classroom register ('high school english class'), missing the emotional point ('missing the overall bigger feelings').

verdicts.trueWording: Claude assumes a heteronormative monogamous interpretation of the interaction instead of what is written
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 6.2, and the source sentence names Claude and carries the 'over what the text actually says' limb as 'instead of what is written'. Corroborated by a writer's comment about 'a hypernormative interpretive framework'.

Quote exact, Sec. 6.2, in the sentence carrying both limbs: 'The action error example in Figure 7 mistakenly states that the narrator decided to stay at the summit. However, "The cold settled into me", is meant to imply that the narrator died at the summit, which was not an action or choice.'

verdicts.trueWording: most faithfulness errors across the models are in Action and Feeling
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 6.2, immediately followed by the claim's second limb verbatim in substance: 'These errors require interpretation of what characters did and how they reacted or felt.' Arithmetic checks: Table 5 faithfulness Action 39 + Feeling 23 = 62 of 104 total.

verdicts.trueWording: summaries rated 4 for analysis actually contain at least one error in analysis on average
verdicts.note: Quote exact, Sec. 6.1. The '4/4' framing is correct: Sec. 5.2 states writers 'rate each of the four attributes on a Likert scale from 1 to 4', and Table 3 gives 1.22 average analysis errors at rating 4. The parenthetical checks against Table 5: Analysis/unsupported 18 + 16 + 70 = 104.
